books.section: Topic 7.4 The Progressives — The Progressive Movement
The Progressive Era and World War I (1900-1920)

primary_sources: Jacob Riis, How the Other Half Lives (1890)

stimulus.source_note: Verbatim excerpt (abridged) from Jacob Riis, How the Other Half Lives (1890), public domain.
stimulus.text: Here is the case of a woman employed in the manufacturing department of a Broadway house. ... She averages three dollars a week. ... lunch she cannot afford. One meal a day is her allowance. ... Almost any door might seem to offer welcome escape from such slavery as this. — Jacob Riis, How the Other Half Lives, 1890 (abridged)

source: original; stimulus paraphrased from 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 20, and Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9
stem: The conditions Riis described most directly pushed Progressive reformers toward

options.misconception: Tariffs were about trade and prices, not about tenement wages or factory conditions.
Railroad trusts were a separate Progressive target; Riis wrote about urban poverty, not railroads.

options.text: expanding the navy and building overseas bases
options.misconception: Naval expansion belonged to the imperialism debate, not to the campaign against urban poverty.

options.text: tenement reform and settlement work in poor neighborhoods

rationales.A: Tariff rates did not feed a woman earning three dollars a week. Riis's problem was urban poverty, not trade policy.
rationales.B: Trust-busting answered monopoly power. Riis's subject was how the poor lived, and the answer lay in housing and neighborhood work.
rationales.C: Overseas bases answered the imperialism debate. Nothing in Riis's passage points toward the navy.
rationales.D: Riis showed middle-class readers how the urban poor actually lived, and reformers answered with tenement laws, settlement houses, and relief work in the neighborhoods he described.
rationales.general:
1. Start with what Riis shows. A woman earning three dollars a week, eating one meal a day, in a crowded city.
2. Ask what reform answers that problem. Tenement reform and settlement houses worked in the poor neighborhoods themselves.
3. Rule out the distant answers. Tariffs, railroad trusts, and the navy belonged to other debates.
Remember: match the reform to the problem's address, because poverty in a tenement is answered in the tenement.
